issue: The clause makes "the other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds" part of the entire agreement without identifying or limiting them. Which documents are inside the integrated whole — and therefore what the parties may prove — cannot be determined from the words.
gold_issue: The phrases “other agreements and instruments executed and delivered” and “entire agreement between the parties relating to the subject matter hereof” were lexically ambiguous as to whether related written agreements were incorporated into an expanded agreement and forum-selection scope or the clause merely barred prior parol evidence.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “the other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds” and the clause’s silence about which documents satisfy that description. G1 turns on that same phrase together with “entire agreement between the parties relating to the subject matter hereof,” asking whether those words incorporate related written agreements or merely exclude prior parol evidence.
evidence: Goldman Sachs countered, however, that the merger clause’s language — stipulating that it covered “instruments executed and delivered” — indicates that it covered more than just any potential oral agreements that may have existed, and-“obyiously ... [included] other written, agreements that deal with the 2004 issuance.”
reason: Both identify uncertainty created by the phrase covering “other agreements and instruments”: the proposed issue questions which writings enter the integrated whole, while g1 questions whether related writings are incorporated at all and thereby expand the agreement and forum-selection scope. G1 is broader and focuses on incorporation’s legal effect rather than solely the documents’ unidentified boundaries.

issue: The disclaimer of "other representations, endorsements, promises, agreements or understandings, oral, written or inferred" is aimed at Goldman's pre-contract Proposal to Provide Investment Banking Services (November 24, 2003), which touted "unparalleled auction rate performance" and that "our clients' interests always come first." Whether the Proposal survives as part of the parties' bargain or is extinguished by this clause is a direct conflict between the two documents.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “there are no other representations, endorsements, promises, agreements or understandings, oral, written or inferred” and its effect on Goldman's November 2003 Proposal. Candidate g1 turns on “other agreements and instruments executed and delivered,” “entire agreement between the parties relating to the subject matter hereof,” and their relationship to the forum-selection clause.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether specific representations in Goldman's pre-contract Proposal were extinguished by the disclaimer. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether executed and delivered related agreements enlarge the integrated agreement and the forum-selection clause’s scope, rather than merely being excluded as parol evidence; that is a different defect involving different operative language.

clause_name: 5.9 Governing Law; Jurisdiction; Waiver of Trial by Jury
issue: Actions "shall be brought in the United States District Court in the County of New York" names a court that does not exist — there is no federal district court "in the County of New York" by that name — and the clause does not say whether it is exclusive or what happens if federal subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking. The venue designation and the mandatory/permissive character of the clause are both open to construction.
gold_issue: The wording “all actions and proceedings ... shall be brought” was disputed as mandatory and exclusive venue language rather than a permissive authorization to litigate in New York.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “shall be brought in the United States District Court in the County of New York,” including both the court designation and whether “shall be brought” makes that forum exclusive. G1 concerns “transactions contemplated hereby”; g2 concerns whether “all actions and proceedings” includes arbitration; g3 concerns whether “all actions and proceedings ... shall be brought” is mandatory and exclusive rather than permissive.
evidence: The forum-séleetion clause is mandatory, because its language cannot be reasonably construed as being permissive.
reason: G3 matches the proposed issue’s complaint that “shall be brought” is open to mandatory/exclusive versus permissive construction. The proposed issue is broader because it also separately challenges the named court’s existence and the clause’s failure to address absent federal subject-matter jurisdiction.

issue: The clause names a State rather than a court, requires the parties to "comply with all requirements necessary to give such court jurisdiction" without identifying any court, and then preserves removal to federal court. Whether it is a binding exclusive forum-selection clause at all is unclear from its own words.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York,” the unclear referent of “such court,” and the sentence preserving removal to federal court. Candidate g1 concerns the conflict between “exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York” and the separate Endorsement’s promise to submit to “any court of competent jurisdiction”; it does not concern the clause’s use of “State,” “such court,” or its removal language as sources of internal uncertainty.
reason: The proposed issue alleges internal uncertainty in the clause’s identification of a forum and its preservation of removal. Candidate g1 instead identifies a conflict with the separate Endorsement and concludes that the Endorsement supplanted an otherwise unambiguous New York forum requirement, so it is not the same defect.

issue: The clause submits the parties to "the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York" while Endorsement 15 promises that, at the insured's request, the company "will submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction". The two cannot both fix the forum.
gold_issue: The promise that the parties “shall submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York” was in whole-contract tension with the Endorsement’s submission to “any court of competent jurisdiction,” and the court held that the Endorsement supplanted the New York forum requirement.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York” and its conflict with Endorsement 15’s “jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction.” Candidate g1 concerns those same two phrases and the same whole-contract conflict, while also recording that the Endorsement displaced the New York requirement.
evidence: Reading the Policy as a whole and giving effect to all of its provisions’ plain meaning, the Court concludes the Service of Suit Endorsement supplants the forum-selection clause and unambiguously permitted Rembrandt to file this action in this Court.
reason: Both identify the same direct conflict between exclusive New York jurisdiction and Endorsement 15’s authorization of any competent court. The candidate additionally states the court’s resolution—that the Endorsement supplanted the forum-selection clause—but that does not change the identity of the defect.

issue: The company's promise to "submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction" at the insured's request cannot be squared with Section IX.I., which commits the parties to the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York. Which provision fixes the forum is a direct conflict.
gold_issue: The promise to “submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction” was disputed as either merely conveying personal jurisdiction or, when the Policy was read as a whole, amending the New York-exclusive forum-selection clause to let the insured choose any competent court.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction” and its conflict with Section IX.I.’s “exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York.” Candidate g1 concerns those same words and the same cross-provision conflict, asking whether the Endorsement merely grants personal jurisdiction or instead amends the New York-exclusive clause.
evidence: The parties provide two possible interpretations of the interplay between the forum-selection clause and the Endorsement. Rembrandt’s interpretation is that the Endorsement is meant as an amendment and thereby changes the Policy’s general jurisdiction and venue terms. (PI. Resp. at 1.) Illinois Union posits that the Endorsement merely conveys personal jurisdiction over it and has no impact on the forum-selection clause. (Def. Reply at 1.)
reason: Both identify the same conflict between the Endorsement’s promise to submit to any competent court and the Policy’s New York-exclusive forum clause. The candidate adds the parties’ competing constructions—personal-jurisdiction consent versus amendment—but addresses the precise defect proposed.

issue: The saving clause says nothing herein varies the Policy's terms "other than as above stated", leaving unresolved whether the endorsement's jurisdiction and service undertakings do override Section IX.I.'s exclusive New York jurisdiction clause. The exception swallows the reservation.
gold_issue: The preservation language “OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED” created a whole-contract coherence question over whether the Endorsement could vary the Policy, and the court read it to permit the stated service-of-suit terms to amend the forum-selection clause.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED” and its effect on the conflict between the endorsement’s jurisdiction/service undertakings and Section IX.I’s exclusive New York clause. Candidate g1 turns on the same exception and the same conflict, describing it as permitting the stated service-of-suit terms to vary the forum-selection clause.
evidence: The Endorsement ends by stating: “NOTHING HEREIN CONTAINED SHALL BE HELD TO VARY, ALTER, WAIVE OR EXTEND ANY OF THE TERMS, CONDITIONS, OR LIMITATIONS OF THE POLICY TO WHIGH THIS ENDORSEMENT IS ATTACHED OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED.” (Id.) (emphasis added). Accordingly, this Court concludes that the plain meaning of this language is quite clear — the Endorsement changes the Policy with respect to the contents of the Endorsément, which indicates that the insured may choose. any competent court in which to sue the insurer.
reason: Both identify the same coherence problem: whether the saving clause’s exception permits the endorsement’s service-of-suit language to override the Policy’s exclusive forum-selection clause. The proposed issue presents the question as unresolved, while g1 records the court’s resolution that the exception allows the amendment.

issue: "Risks of direct physical loss or damage" is undefined and its boundary — whether cosmetic, functional or merely diminished-value harm counts as "direct physical loss or damage" — is the classic battleground of an all-risk grant. The phrase "unless excluded" also leaves the burden and reach of the exclusions to be worked out.
gold_issue: The phrase “direct physical loss or damage” was alleged to be lexically ambiguous between any physical alteration, including cosmetic hail dents, and only damage measurably reducing the property’s usefulness or function.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “risks of direct physical loss or damage,” particularly its coverage of cosmetic, functional, or diminished-value harm, and separately “unless excluded.” Candidate g1 concerns the lexical scope of “direct physical loss or damage” as between cosmetic alteration and functional impairment; g2 instead concerns whether that grant is narrowed by the separate “covered loss” provisions in the Coverages section.
evidence: Defendant cites several cases for the proposition that “physical loss or damage” requires a showing of a measurable reduction in the property’s usefulness or a change to an unsatisfactory state. These cases, however, do not apply directly to the interpretation of the phrase “physical loss or damage” in this Policy. Against the backdrop of Advance Cable and other persuasive authority that suggests that “physical loss or damage” includes cosmetic hail damage that physically alters an insured’s property, the Court is not convinced that the cases offered by Defendant define the phrase to mean functional damage.
reason: The proposed issue and g1 identify the same disputed boundary of “direct physical loss or damage”: whether cosmetic physical alteration suffices or functional/usefulness impairment is required. The proposal’s additional concern about “unless excluded” is not covered by g1, but does not undermine the direct match on its principal defect.

issue: The grant covers real property "at or within one-thousand (1,000) feet of a covered location," so its whole reach depends on the contested identification of covered locations under the Schedule (c028) and DEFINITIONS E. (c214). Property at an unlisted address may or may not fall within the grant.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “at or within one-thousand (1,000) feet of a covered location” and the identification of “covered locations” through the Schedule and DEFINITIONS E. Candidate g1 concerns the lexical meaning of “covered loss”; candidate g2 concerns whether “covered loss” limits the separate “physical loss or damage” grant.
reason: Neither candidate names the proposed location-identification defect. Both concern the meaning or limiting effect of “covered loss,” whereas the proposed issue concerns whether an address qualifies as “a covered location.”

issue: "Covered loss" is confined to loss "at a covered location," although the Insuring Agreement (c009) and COVERAGES A. and B. (c029, c030) extend to property within 1,000 feet of, or in transit away from, a covered location. The definition and those grants describe different geographic reach.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “at a covered location” and its conflict with grants covering property within 1,000 feet of or in transit away from that location. g1 turns on the words “a loss” and whether they exclude cosmetic damage; g2 turns on “covered loss” as an asserted limitation on “physical loss or damage” and the absence of the enumerated-list/general-term structure required for ejusdem generis.
reason: Neither candidate names the geographic inconsistency alleged by the proposed issue. g1 concerns whether “a loss” requires functional damage, while g2 concerns whether the definition limits the broader phrase “physical loss or damage” and whether ejusdem generis supports that limitation; neither addresses the mismatch between “at a covered location” and coverage extending beyond that location.

issue: 3.3's allowance that consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions" and inferred from circumstances cannot be squared with 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" for each act of sexual contact. A fact-finder applying both has no rule for consent manifested by conduct in an ongoing relationship.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on § 3.3’s words “may be communicated verbally or through actions,” contrasted with § 3.1’s “explicit consent” requirement, particularly for consent manifested by conduct in an ongoing relationship. Candidate g1 turns on § 3.3’s statement that an existing sexual relationship “does not constitute consent,” its relationship to consent communicated “through actions,” and whether that relationship is nevertheless relevant context.
reason: The proposed issue alleges a conflict between § 3.3 and § 3.1’s separate requirement of explicit consent for each act. Candidate g1 instead concerns an alleged internal tension within § 3.3 and whether the prior relationship may remain relevant context despite not itself constituting consent, so it does not name the same defect.

issue: The prohibited behaviors — "intimidates", "harasses or bullies", "unwanted physical contact", "endangers the health, safety, or welfare" — are stated as bare verbs with no severity, intent, or reasonableness threshold. A student cannot tell from the words where ordinary conduct ends and a violation begins.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the bare terms “intimidates,” “harasses or bullies,” “unwanted physical contact,” and “endangers the health, safety, or welfare,” specifically their silence as to severity, intent, and reasonableness. Candidate g1 concerns “physically harms or is considered unwanted physical contact” together with the examples “hitting, pushing, or physical altercations/violence of any kind,” and whether that wording classifies nonviolent unwanted sexual contact as “violence.”
reason: The proposed issue alleges that several prohibitions lack severity, intent, or reasonableness thresholds. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether the examples and reference to “violence” bring nonviolent unwanted sexual contact within § 2.1.d, a distinct list-scope and definitional problem.

clause_name: Section 9: Cost of Insurance Charge basis
issue: The rate factors are enumerated — sex, Age, Risk Classification, Basic and Supplemental Face Amount, Net Amount at Risk and duration — and expressio unius would make that list exhaustive, so that rates may not be set by reference to unlisted characteristics. The sentence is also expressly limited to rates "as of the Policy Date," saying nothing about later re-determinations.
gold_issue: The scope of “as of the Policy Date” was unclear until Paragraph A was construed together with Paragraph B, which made Paragraph A govern only the initial COI rate and Paragraph B govern subsequent Policy-Month adjustments.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns both the enumerated factor list and its silence about unlisted characteristics, and the phrase “as of the Policy Date” and its silence about later rate determinations. G1 concerns the omission of “Policy Value” from that list and its incorporation through the separately defined “Net Amount at Risk,” while g2 concerns “as of the Policy Date” read against Paragraph B’s “Policy Month” language for later adjustments.
evidence: Paragraph A specifically states that its factors are to be used in setting the COI rate on the “Policy Date,” and Paragraph B enumerates the factors to be used in setting the COI rate for a “Policy Month.” Given these two separate COI rate definitions, the contract must be interpreted to mean that only the initial COI rate is calculated in accordance with Paragraph A. Any subsequent COI rate adjustments — COI rates for “Policy Months”— must be calculated in accordance with Paragraph B.
reason: G2 directly matches the proposed issue’s temporal-scope complaint: “as of the Policy Date” limits this sentence to the initial rate and leaves later adjustments to other text. The choice is somewhat close because g1 touches the proposed list-exhaustiveness theory, but g1 specifically concerns Policy Value’s incorporation through Net Amount at Risk rather than whether all unlisted characteristics are excluded.

issue: Rates "will be based on our expectations of future mortality, persistency, investment earnings, expense experience, capital and reserve requirements, and tax assumptions" — a list of unquantified factors with no stated weighting or benchmark, and "based on" fixes no relationship between expectations and rates. Whether a rate increase is permitted by this language is precisely what an insured would litigate.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue targets “will be based on our expectations of” and the provision’s silence about how the listed factors are weighted or translated into rates. g1 targets whether “based on” makes the list exclusive; g2 targets “mortality”; g3 targets “persistency”; g4 targets “expectations of ... investment earnings” and whether earnings means income or spread; and g5 targets “specific Policy Month” in contrast with Paragraph A’s “Policy Date.”
reason: No recorded defect names the proposed omission of a weighting, benchmark, formula, or required relationship between Phoenix’s expectations and the resulting rate. Although g1 also concerns “based on,” it addresses whether the enumerated list is exhaustive, not how those factors must determine or justify a rate increase; g4 instead disputes the meaning of “investment earnings.”

issue: The factors listed here differ from the factors listed in the immediately preceding Cost of Insurance Charge sentence (sex, Age, Risk Classification, face amounts, Net Amount at Risk, duration), and the policy never says how the two lists relate. An insured would argue the earlier, closed list limits the factors usable under this one.
gold_issue: The reference to a “specific Policy Month” was construed together with Paragraph A’s separate reference to the “Policy Date,” resulting in Paragraph B governing COI-rate adjustments after the initial rate was set.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the difference and alleged silence between Paragraph A’s list—sex, Age, Risk Classification, face amounts, Net Amount at Risk, and duration—and Paragraph B’s “based on our expectations of” list. g1 concerns “based on”; g2 “mortality”; g3 “persistency”; g4 “expectations of ... investment earnings”; and g5 the interaction between “specific Policy Month” and Paragraph A’s “Policy Date,” which determines how the two factor lists apply.
evidence: Paragraph A specifically states that its factors are to be used in setting the COI rate on the “Policy Date,” and Paragraph B enumerates the factors to be used in setting the COI rate for a “Policy Month.” Given these two separate COI rate definitions, the contract must be interpreted to mean that only the initial COI rate is calculated in accordance with Paragraph A. Any subsequent COI rate adjustments — COI rates for “Policy Months”— must be calculated in accordance with Paragraph B.
reason: Both concern how the preceding factor list and the current factor list relate. The proposed issue treats that relationship as unstated and argues that the earlier list limits the later sentence, while g5 resolves it through the “Policy Date”/“Policy Month” distinction, making the earlier list govern the initial rate and the current list govern later adjustments.

clause_name: Section 9: Cost of Insurance rate changes
issue: Re-determination is permitted "on a basis that does not discriminate unfairly within any class of insureds," but "class of insureds" is undefined and the insurer alone would draw the class boundaries. Whether a rate increase applied to a sub-group (by face amount or issue age) is within "any class" is the core construction question.
gold_issue: The phrase “class of insureds” was vague about whether classes had to be fixed at policy issuance or Phoenix could later subdivide the issued PAUL series by age and face amount.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “class of insureds” and the provision’s silence about who defines class boundaries, particularly for age- or face-amount subgroups. G1 instead concerns “discriminate unfairly” and what makes differential treatment unfair; g2 concerns “class of insureds” and the silence about whether issuance classes could later be subdivided by age and face amount.
evidence: Fleisher also argues that Phoenix was required to define any “class of insureds” at the time of policy issuance. Thus, Fle-isher reasons, the groupings Phoenix identified at issuance — the PAUL IIIA and PAUL IIIB/C policy series — constituted the relevant “classes.” Fleisher contends that Phoenix was not permitted to further subdivide the existing policy series classes by age and face amount and to treat each subdivision differently.
reason: The proposed issue and g2 identify the same ambiguity: who may define a “class of insureds” and whether Phoenix could subdivide existing policy series by age and face amount. G2 adds the more specific question whether classes had to be fixed at issuance, but that is a direct formulation of the proposed boundary-drawing problem.

clause_name: Section 9: Cost of Insurance rate changes
issue: "We will not distribute past gains or recoup prior losses, if any, by changing the rates" gives no test for distinguishing a permitted prospective re-pricing from a forbidden recoupment of losses already incurred. The sentence's coverage of an increase driven by past adverse experience is genuinely doubtful.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “We will not distribute past gains or recoup prior losses, if any, by changing the rates,” particularly its silence on how to identify forbidden recoupment. Candidate g1 concerns “discriminate unfairly,” while g2 concerns “class of insureds” and whether a class may be redefined after issuance.
reason: Neither candidate addresses the proposed distinction between permissible prospective rate changes and forbidden recoupment of prior losses. Both concern separate ambiguities in the unfair-discrimination condition.

issue: The parenthetical "(not including the laws which might apply the laws of another jurisdiction)" is garbled and its intended exclusion of renvoi/conflicts rules must be reconstructed. "Any dispute" is also undefined as to whether it reaches tort and statutory claims as well as contract claims.
gold_issue: Brenner challenged “any dispute” as lexically ambiguous, but offered no competing reading and the court rejected the asserted ambiguity.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue targets both the parenthetical “(not including the laws which might apply the laws of another jurisdiction)” as garbled and “Any dispute” as uncertain in claim-type scope. g1 targets “governed by the substantive laws ... of the State of Wyoming” and its silence about the threshold choice-of-law inquiry, while g2 targets “any dispute” and its alleged lexical ambiguity.
evidence: Brenner next argues that the contract is ambiguous because it refers to “any dispute.” Brenner does not explain, however, any way in which such language is ambiguous, and such an argument is also without merit.
reason: Both the proposed issue and g2 identify ambiguity in the scope of “any dispute”; the proposed issue merely supplies a specific possible uncertainty—whether noncontractual claims are included—that the litigant apparently did not articulate. The proposed parenthetical/renvoi concern is separate and does not match g1’s concern about the clause’s failure expressly to govern the threshold choice-of-law inquiry.

issue: "Shall occur or be filed only in the State of Wyoming" does not say whether suit must be in Wyoming state court or may be in the federal court sitting there, and does not say whether mediation is a mandatory condition precedent to suit. The clause's mandatory reach and its forum are both open on these words.
gold_issue: The phrase requiring suit “only in the State of Wyoming” did not specify federal or state court, and the court construed it to permit suit in either court located there.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns both “only in the State of Wyoming,” specifically its silence about federal versus state court, and “any mediation or suit shall occur or be filed,” specifically its silence about mandatory mediation before suit. g1 concerns the breadth of “any mediation or suit” as applied to noncontract tort claims, while g2 concerns the federal-versus-state-court silence in “only in the State of Wyoming.”
evidence: “The fact that the provision does not specify federal or state court does not make it invalid, but rather allows suit to be brought in either court.”
reason: The proposed issue and g2 identify the same silence in “only in the State of Wyoming”: neither wording specifies state rather than federal court. The score is slightly below full alignment because the proposed issue additionally raises a separate, unmatched question about whether mediation is a condition precedent.

issue: The transportation carve-out is grammatically broken ("Any deduction for the expenses ... shall be added to the price received" with an unclosed parenthetical reading "limited to direct for amounts of Lessor's gas transported"), so the scope of the permitted regulated-pipeline deduction cannot be read off the words. Whether "gathering" and "compression" charged by an affiliate midstream company fall inside or outside the no-deduction rule is the central ambiguity.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the second sentence’s exception for regulated-pipeline transportation charges, particularly “limited to direct for amounts of Lessor's gas transported,” and on whether “gathering” and “compression” by an affiliate remain nondeductible. Candidate g1 turns on the relationship between the actual-proceeds formula, the transportation-expense sentence, and a separate third sentence requiring proceeds to equal or exceed field or prevailing-area proceeds.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the transportation exception itself is grammatically indeterminate and leaves affiliate gathering and compression charges uncertain. Candidate g1 instead concerns which earlier sentence a separate minimum-proceeds sentence modifies, so it does not name the same defect.

issue: The royalty base is "proceeds received from any sale of such gas at the point of sale or delivery," which sits against Paragraph 3(f)'s command that royalties be delivered free of gathering, compression, treating and marketing costs "except as provided for in 3(b)." The two must be reconciled to know whether the valuation point can be moved downstream by netting costs out of the sale price.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “proceeds received from any sale of such gas at the point of sale or delivery,” the expense-deduction language in 3(b), and 3(f)’s “except as provided for in 3(b)” cross-reference. Candidate g1 turns on the relationship among 3(b)’s actual-proceeds sentence, transportation-expense sentence, and a separate minimum-proceeds sentence requiring comparison with sales “in the field or prevailing area whichever is greater.”
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether 3(b), read with 3(f), permits a downstream valuation point and netting of post-production costs. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether an internal minimum-proceeds sentence modifies the actual-proceeds formula or the preceding transportation-expense sentence, so it identifies a different textual conflict.

issue: The floor is set by "proceeds received from sales in the field or prevailing area whichever is the greater," and neither "field" nor "prevailing area" is defined or bounded. Nor is it said whose sales, over what period, are to be compared.
gold_issue: The undefined phrase “field or prevailing area” was lexically ambiguous because Dorchester treated “field” and “prevailing area” as two different localities, whereas Chesapeake treated them as a single, roughly synonymous geographic term.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “proceeds received from sales in the field or prevailing area whichever is the greater,” particularly the undefined geographic terms and the silence about whose sales and the comparison period. Candidate g1 concerns “field or prevailing area” and whether those words denote two different localities or one synonymous geographic term; g2 concerns the whole minimum-proceeds sentence and its relationship to the preceding royalty language, the oil formula, payment timing, and paragraph 3(d)’s cross-reference.
evidence: Central to the dispute is the meaning of the phrase “field or prevailing area.” According to Dorchester, “field” refers to the locality where production occurs, whereas “prevailing area” refers to the point of sale. Chesapeake disagrees, contending that “field or prevailing area” is a single term in which “field” and “prevailing area” are more or less synonymous, as in the phrase “cardinal or red.”
reason: The proposed issue and g1 both identify uncertainty in the undefined phrase “field or prevailing area,” but g1 focuses specifically on whether it denotes one locality or two, while the proposed issue emphasizes geographic bounds and missing comparator details such as whose sales and what period. They therefore describe the same underlying ambiguity, with the proposed issue adding omissions not captured by g1.

issue: Performance continues during a dispute "unless otherwise directed by MTC," a unilateral power given to one Party over obligations that run both ways, with no equivalent for the Network Operator and no statement of whether MTC may thereby suspend its own duties. The scope of that direction is the operative uncertainty.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “unless otherwise directed by MTC” and the silence about the scope of MTC’s direction, including whether it reaches MTC’s own duties. Candidate g1 turns on Section 11.2 as a whole and the Guaranty’s cross-reference to “[a]ll other provisions relating to dispute resolution,” not on the MTC-direction clause.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the scope and asymmetry of MTC’s unilateral authority to direct otherwise. The recorded defect instead concerns whether Section 11.2 as a whole is incorporated into the Guaranty as an “other provision relating to dispute resolution,” so it is a different defect.

issue: The choice-of-law sentence says the Guaranty is governed "exclusively" by Massachusetts law, while the dispute-resolution provisions of the Network Operator Agreement incorporated by the last sentence of Section 4.6 provide for decision under Massachusetts law "and any applicable federal law." A court could be asked whether "exclusively" displaces federal law, including the Federal Arbitration Act.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “governed by, construed in and enforced in accordance exclusively with the laws of the State of Massachusetts” and its asserted conflict with incorporated language allowing “any applicable federal law.” Candidate g1 turns on the heading “Governing Law, Jurisdiction, Venue and Forum,” the placement of the incorporation language within §4.6 rather than Article II, and whether that organization precludes an additional dispute-related covenant.
reason: The proposed issue alleges a conflict over whether the exclusive Massachusetts choice-of-law clause displaces federal law. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether §4.6’s heading and placement prevent its incorporated dispute-resolution language from creating an enforceable performance covenant; it is a different defect.

issue: The clause conditions arbitration and litigation on the parties failing "to resolve any dispute between them through mediation, or [being] unable to convene mediation within 60 days," yet nothing in the Guaranty (or in NOA Article 11, which provides for IPT negotiation and arbitration) creates any mediation obligation or procedure. The precondition therefore has no defined content or trigger.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “fail to resolve any dispute between them through mediation” and “unable to convene mediation within 60 days,” together with the alleged silence concerning any mediation obligation or procedure. Candidate g1 turns on “All other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration contained in the Network Operator Agreement are incorporated herein by reference,” particularly whether that language incorporates §11.2 despite §4.6’s distinct procedures.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the mediation language creates an undefined precondition because neither agreement supplies a mediation obligation or procedure. Candidate g1 instead concerns the scope and effect of the final sentence’s incorporation of other Network Operator Agreement dispute-resolution provisions, including §11.2, so it names a different defect.

issue: The final sentence incorporates "[a]ll other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration contained in the Network Operator Agreement," but NOA Article 11 makes IPT escalation and binding arbitration a mandatory condition precedent to any suit, which cannot be squared with this section's scheme of litigation in Middlesex County unless MTC elects arbitration. A court would have to decide which regime controls a dispute with the Guarantor.
gold_issue: The phrase “All other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration” was disputed as to whether it incorporated Network Operator Agreement §11.2 despite §4.6’s differing dispute procedures, and the court construed the specific variations as carve-outs while giving the residual incorporation language effect.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “All other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration,” read against the preceding MTC-election and Middlesex County litigation language and the Network Operator Agreement’s asserted mandatory escalation/arbitration terms. G1 turns on the same incorporation phrase and preceding procedures, but specifically asks whether they permit incorporation of Network Operator Agreement §11.2 despite the agreements’ differing procedures.
evidence: Further, while Axia NetMedia suggests MTC is picking and choosing which dispute resolution provisions are incorporated by reference into the Guaranty, and points out that the Guaranty provides for particular dispute resolution procedures that contradict those in the Network Operator Agreement, the specific language of Section 4.6 of the Guaranty carved out these specific variations to the dispute resolution process, and clearly stated that the incorporation by reference was for “[a]ll other provisions relating to dispute resolution....”
reason: Both identify the underlying conflict between §4.6’s specific mediation, arbitration-election, and litigation procedures and its residual incorporation of the Network Operator Agreement’s dispute-resolution provisions. The match is partial because the proposed issue specifically invokes Article 11’s mandatory escalation and arbitration regime, whereas g1 specifically concerns incorporation of §11.2, the “Continued Performance” provision.

issue: "The next salary adjustment is scheduled for April 1, 2015" is ambiguous as to whether it promises an increase on that date or merely a review, given the preceding sentence making adjustment discretionary with the Board. "Annual review for adjustment" sets no benchmark or direction for the adjustment.
gold_issue: The phrase “subject to annual review for adjustment at the discretion of the Board,” together with the scheduled next adjustment, was alleged to require a salary review or adjustment but was construed as unambiguously giving the Board discretion not to consider or modify Lankau’s compensation.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “subject to annual review for adjustment at the discretion of the Board,” the sentence scheduling the next adjustment for April 1, 2015, and the absence of a benchmark or direction for adjustment. Candidate g1 concerns the same discretionary-review phrase together with the scheduled-adjustment sentence, asking whether those words require review or modification despite the Board’s discretion.
evidence: A similar issue is present as to the salary adjustment review, which includes a provision noting such review is “at the discretion of the Board.”
reason: Both identify the tension between the scheduled “next salary adjustment” and the Board’s discretion over annual review and adjustment—specifically, whether the language creates an obligation to review or increase salary. The proposed issue additionally notes the absence of an adjustment benchmark, which the recorded defect does not separately address.

issue: Eligibility to participate in the "Stock Option Plan (subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation's policies)" makes the benefit wholly contingent, and no Stock Option Plan is identified or attached. Whether the clause confers anything is a question of construction.
gold_issue: The parenthetical “subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation’s policies” was facially ambiguous because it could modify Lankau’s eligibility for an individual equity grant, as Luxoft argued, or refer only to Board approval of SOP III, as Lankau argued.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “Stock Option Plan (subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation’s policies)” and the provision’s silence as to an identified or attached plan. Candidate g1 concerns the same parenthetical, specifically what “subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation’s policies” modifies: individual grant eligibility or approval of SOP III.
evidence: From the face of the Employment Agreement, the equity compensation provision could reasonably support both sides’ positions. The language of the parenthetical can plausibly be read to indicate that the only limit to Plaintiff receiving equity is approval of the stock options plan by the Board, as Plaintiff posits. It can also be reasonably read as Defendants suggest.
reason: Both defects concern whether the approval parenthetical makes the executive’s eligibility for equity contingent, but g1 identifies the more precise ambiguity: whether approval modifies the individual grant or only the plan. The proposed issue instead asserts wholesale contingency and adds a separate concern that no plan is identified or attached.

words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “reserves the right to escalate” and the provision’s silence about exercise, notice, timing, and whether escalation is automatic or elective. Candidate g1 turns on “oil and/or gas,” specifically the scope of “gas” and whether that term includes NGLs.
reason: The proposed issue concerns uncertainty over how and when Farmor may exercise the reserved right to escalate the royalty. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether “gas” includes liquid NGLs, so it identifies a different term and a different alleged defect.

issue: The proportionate-reduction sentence is garbled — "if Farmor's interest in the acreage is less than one hundred percent (100%) or the working interest" — so the trigger for reduction cannot be read as written. words_at_issue: The proposed issue targets the proportionate-reduction wording “if Farmor's interest in the acreage is less than one hundred percent (100%) or the working interest” and the silence of “gross proceeds ... without deductions of any kind” regarding post-production costs.
