issue: The first sentence puts "all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss" on the Participant while the last sentence puts on the Bank "the risk of loss arising from negligent and freudvlent operation of its Securities Lending Program", and the two cannot both be given their full scope. "Negligent and fraudulent" is also ambiguous as to whether negligence alone suffices, and "operation of its Securities Lending Program" does not say whether collateral investment is part of that operation.
gold_issue: The word “operation” in Wells Fargo’s assumption of losses from negligent operation of the Securities Lending Program was unclear as to whether it included investment of the cash collateral.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the interaction between “collateral investment loss” and “negligent and freudvlent operation of its Securities Lending Program,” especially whether “operation” includes collateral investment and whether “and” requires both negligence and fraud. g1 concerns whether “collateral investment loss” reaches investments violating SLA criteria; g2 concerns whether “operation” includes investing cash collateral; g3 concerns the SLA’s negligence language conflicting with the Declaration’s gross-negligence standard; and g4 concerns “collateral deficiencies” in relation to returning collateral or loaned securities.
evidence: Wells Fargo contends that the negligence standard of the SLA does not apply because it imposes liability on Wells Fargo only with respect to the “operation” of the Securities Lending Program, which does not include the investment of the collateral. It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue and g2 both question whether “operation of its Securities Lending Program” includes collateral investment, thereby determining how the Participant’s collateral-investment-loss assumption overlaps with the Bank’s negligence liability. The proposed issue additionally raises the meaning of “negligent and fraudulent,” which g2 does not cover; g1 concerns adjacent language but specifically asks whether “collateral investment loss” includes investments violating the SLA’s criteria.

issue: Section 8's assignment of all collateral-investment loss to the Participant cannot be squared with Section 2(f), which commits the Bank to invest cash collateral only in the listed short-term instruments with safety of principal and liquidity as prime considerations. A court must decide whether Section 8 excuses losses caused by investments outside the Section 2(f) mandate.
gold_issue: The phrase “collateral investment loss” was unclear as to whether COPIC assumed losses caused by Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that failed to meet the SLA’s investment criteria.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “collateral investment loss” and its interaction with Section 2(f)’s investment mandate; g1 concerns that same phrase and the same investment criteria. By contrast, g2 concerns “operation,” g3 concerns the negligent-operation sentence’s conflict with the Declaration’s gross-negligence threshold, and g4 concerns “collateral deficiencies” and the timing of funding a shortfall relative to returning securities.
evidence: I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue and g1 both ask whether “collateral investment loss” shifts to the Participant losses caused by investments that violated the SLA’s investment criteria. They therefore identify essentially the same defect, with the proposed issue expressly framing it as a conflict with Section 2(f).

issue: "Directly competitive" is not defined and there is no benchmark (product function, customer, catalog listing) for deciding when a line the Representative carries competes with a Lovejoy product. Because the authorized products in section 1 expand with "subsequent catalogs," the reach of the restraint moves with the Company's publications.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the undefined phrase “directly competitive” and on “any product the Representative is to offer, promote or sell for the Company,” as allegedly expanded through section 1’s “subsequent catalogs.” Candidate g1 concerns the prohibition as a whole in combination with the separate House Accounts provision and Lovejoy’s claimed “unfettered” account-designation power.
reason: The proposed issue alleges indeterminacy in identifying competitive products and a changing product universe. Candidate g1 instead alleges that the noncompete becomes oppressive when combined with Lovejoy’s asserted power to redesignate substantially all accounts as House Accounts; that is a different whole-contract conflict, not uncertainty about product competitiveness or catalog expansion.

issue: "House Account" is never defined and the Company "reserves the right to redefine these accounts" with no notice requirement or limit, so accounts earning commission can be moved out of commission unilaterally. Addendum A is described only as a "current roster," leaving the operative list a moving target.
gold_issue: The words “reserves the right to redefine these accounts” could not coherently grant Lovejoy an “unfettered” right to designate all or substantially all accounts as House Accounts when the Agreement was read as a whole, because that construction would annul the termination scheme and preserve the noncompetition restraint while depriving Kamco of its benefits.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the undefined term “House Account,” the words “reserves the right to redefine these accounts,” the absence of notice or limits, and Addendum A’s description as a “current roster.” g1 principally turns on “reserves the right to redefine these accounts,” construed against the Agreement’s termination scheme and noncompetition restraint.
evidence: The more significant problem with Love-joy’s argument that it had an “unfettered” right to redefine the House Accounts is that this interpretation would nullify portions of the Agreement’s termination provision.
reason: Both identify the same core defect: the ostensibly unrestricted unilateral power to redefine House Accounts could remove accounts from Kamco’s commission base and deprive it of contractual benefits. The proposed issue additionally emphasizes the undefined term, lack of notice, and “current roster,” while g1 focuses on why an unfettered construction conflicts with the termination and noncompetition provisions.

issue: Termination for cause requires the "other party's unreasonable and repeated failure to perform," a standard that is undefined and doubly qualified, and the notice sentence is grammatically broken ("mailed via certified or registered to") so the sequence of notice, cure and termination is uncertain. A court would have to construe what conduct and what notice suffice.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns subsection 16(c)(i), particularly “unreasonable and repeated failure to perform” and the malformed phrase “mailed via certified or registered to,” which govern cause, notice, cure, and termination. Candidate g1 concerns the annual-renewal and sixty-day-notice sentence, the “mutual written agreement” term, and their conflict with Lovejoy’s asserted power under the separate House Accounts provision.
reason: The proposed issue alleges ambiguity within the for-cause standard and its notice-and-cure procedure. Candidate g1 instead identifies a conflict whereby Lovejoy’s reading of the separate House Accounts provision would circumvent and nullify the termination scheme; it does not identify uncertainty in the for-cause language or notice grammar.

issue: The termination provision says nothing about commissions on orders accepted or shipped after termination, which must be read against section 7's limit of credit to "as long as this Agreement remains in force" and section 8's payment 45 days after the month of shipment. The parties' post-termination positions emerge only from reading the three together.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on section 16’s silence about commissions for orders accepted or shipped after termination, read with section 7’s phrase “as long as this Agreement remains in force” and section 8’s shipment-based payment timing. Candidate g1 turns on the annual-renewal and sixty-day-notice language, the enumerated termination grounds, and “mutual written agreement,” asserting a conflict with Lovejoy’s claimed power under the House Accounts provision to reclassify every account.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the absence of any rule governing post-termination commissions and its interaction with sections 7 and 8. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether Lovejoy’s reading of the House Accounts provision would circumvent and nullify the enumerated termination methods; it is a different defect despite involving the same termination provision.

issue: The guaranty runs "to each Trustee for the benefit of each Holder," but Endorsement No. 1 defines the Trustee as U.S. Bank while making Wells Fargo the Trust Administrator, and PSA Sections 12.04 and 12.06 give the Trust Administrator alone the power to claim on and hold the Policy. Who the guaranty is owed to, and who may enforce it, cannot be settled from this provision alone.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “to each Trustee” and its conflict with Endorsement No. 1 and PSA Sections 12.04 and 12.06 assigning policy-related authority to the Trust Administrator. Candidate g1 concerns “for the benefit of each Holder,” specifically whether “Holder” includes holders of Uninsured Certificates or only Insured Certificates.
reason: No candidate records the alleged conflict between the named Trustee and the Trust Administrator’s exclusive authority to claim on and hold the Policy. Candidate g1 instead concerns which certificateholders qualify as “Holder,” specifically insured versus uninsured certificateholders, so it is a different defect despite involving the same guaranty clause.

issue: After identifying reimbursement 'with interest' for claims paid, the definition adds 'any amounts with respect to the Class 1-A-3 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid,' an open-ended catch-all not tied to any enumerated obligation. The class of amounts it sweeps in is unbounded.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the trailing words “any amounts with respect to the Class 1-A-3 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid,” alleging that they are not limited to enumerated obligations. Candidate g1 concerns the separate definition of the entire “Class 1-A-3 Certificate Insurer Reimbursement Amount” and its asserted redundancy in light of section 4.02(a)(3) and later waterfall steps, not the breadth of the trailing catch-all.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the definition’s final catch-all is substantively unbounded. Candidate g1 instead identifies a redundancy or whole-contract coherence problem arising from Assured’s interpretation of section 4.02(a)(3), so it does not record the same defect.

issue: The closing phrase 'any amounts with respect to the Class 2-A-3 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid' is a general catch-all appended to the specific reimbursement-with-interest item. Nothing in the definition limits what obligations qualify as 'owing.'
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the closing words “any amounts with respect to the Class 2-A-3 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid,” particularly the absence of a limitation on “owing.” Candidate g1 concerns the separate definition as a whole and its asserted redundancy under section 4.02(a)(3), not the breadth of the closing phrase.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the definition’s closing catch-all lacks a limiting principle for obligations “owing” to the insurer. Candidate g1 instead identifies redundancy between the separately defined class-specific reimbursement amount and Assured’s interpretation of the payment waterfall in section 4.02(a)(3), so it is a different defect.

issue: The clause 'any amounts with respect to the Class 4-A-2 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid' extends the reimbursement amount beyond the enumerated claims paid under the Policy without any stated boundary. Its scope against the specific preceding item is open to construction.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the definition’s concluding words, “any amounts with respect to the Class 4-A-2 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid,” and their relationship to the preceding Policy-claims language. Candidate g1 concerns the separately defined term as a whole and its asserted redundancy when read alongside section 4.02(a)(3) and later waterfall steps, not the scope of that concluding phrase.
reason: The proposed issue alleges an internally unbounded catch-all that may expand the reimbursement amount beyond Policy claims. The candidate instead alleges that section 4.02(a)(3), under Assured’s interpretation, makes the separately defined class-specific amount unnecessary in later waterfall steps; that is a different whole-contract redundancy defect.

issue: The waterfall pays the Certificate Insurer its Premium Distribution Amount and Aggregate Certificate Insurer Reimbursement Amount ahead of Mezzanine interest and principal, and pays Unpaid Realized Loss Amounts on the Class 1-A-3, 2-A-3 and 4-A-2 Certificates only 'to the extent not covered by the Certificate Insurance Policy,' which requires reading the priorities against the Policy and Endorsement No. 1 and the deemed-balance proviso in the definition of Certificate Principal Balance. Whether insured holders or the insurer are entitled to a given dollar cannot be determined from this section alone.
gold_issue: The phrase in section 4.02(a)(3) directing payment to Assured “up to the Aggregate Certificate Insurer Reimbursement Amount” was susceptible to Assured’s reading as a separate right to reimbursement for all principal and interest claims and the certificateholders’ reading as payment only of amounts arising through subrogation.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “Premium Distribution Amount” in clause (2)(B), “Aggregate Certificate Insurer Reimbursement Amount” in clause (3), and clause (8)’s “to the extent not covered by the Certificate Insurance Policy,” read with the Policy, Endorsement No. 1, and the Certificate Principal Balance definition. G1 concerns specifically “up to the Aggregate Certificate Insurer Reimbursement Amount” in clause (3) and whether it creates reimbursement independent of section 12.05 and Policy subrogation; g2 concerns that same clause’s relationship to the sixteen later insurer-payment steps, the class-specific reimbursement definitions, and section 12.05.
evidence:
According to Assured, this “reimbursement” right under 4.02(a)(3) is separate and independent from its right of subrogation. The right of subrogation is contained in PSA section 12.05 and in the Policy.
Certificateholder Defendants deny that 4.02(a)(3) grants Assured a separate reimbursement right. They argue that the Trust documents only permit Assured to collect funds that arise from its subrogation to the certificates it insures, to wit, any amount that would otherwise be paid to the Senior Support certificateholders had they not given up their rights to it.
reason: The proposed issue’s uncertainty over whether insured holders or the insurer receives funds, particularly through the priority given the Aggregate Certificate Insurer Reimbursement Amount, substantially tracks g1’s dispute over whether section 4.02(a)(3) grants broad reimbursement or only subrogation-based payments. G1 is closer than g2 because the proposed issue does not specifically allege that a broad reading makes the sixteen later insurer-payment steps meaningless, though it also invokes additional provisions not central to g1.

clause_name: 12.05 Effect of Policy payments and subrogation
issue: Payments made with Policy moneys 'shall not result in the payment of or the provision for the payment of the principal of or interest on such Insured Certificate within the meaning of Section 4.01,' although Section 4.01 governs Advances and distributions to Certificateholders are made under Section 4.02. The deeming rule that keeps the insured certificates outstanding is anchored to the wrong section.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the first sentence’s cross-reference “within the meaning of Section 4.01” and claims that Section 4.02 was intended. Candidate g1 turns on clause (ii), particularly “only from the sources and in the manner provided herein,” and its relationship to the Section 4.02 waterfall and the subrogation right in clause (i).
reason: The proposed issue alleges an erroneous cross-reference that anchors the certificate-outstanding deeming rule to Section 4.01 instead of Section 4.02. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether the separate “sources and manner provided herein” language makes waterfall payments an implementation of subrogation or an independent reimbursement right, so it records a different defect.

issue: Clause (iv) bars participation in "any business in which he would be reasonably likely to employ, reveal, or otherwise utilize Trade Secrets" in "any geographical area in which the Company or any of its affiliates conduct business," a restraint whose reach depends on a speculative likelihood judgment rather than any identified line of business. Clause (ii)'s flat bar on hiring any current or recent employee is also untethered to any solicitation by Employee.
gold_issue: The phrase “reasonably likely” in the prohibition on participating in a business likely to use Aspect’s trade secrets was challenged as lexically vague and unenforceable or ambiguous enough to require extrinsic evidence, although the court found little support for either reading.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns clause (iv)’s words “any business in which he would be reasonably likely to employ, reveal, or otherwise utilize Trade Secrets,” especially “reasonably likely” and the absence of an identified line of business; it also separately concerns clause (ii)’s bar on hiring “any person” who is a current or recent employee. Candidate g1 concerns only the phrase “reasonably likely” in clause (iv), alleging that it is vague or ambiguous.
evidence: Instead of quarreling with the scope and breadth of the non-compete clause, Barnett argues that the phrase “reasonably likely” is either vague and therefore unenforceable or ambiguous and therefore requiring the Court to resort to extrinsic evidence to determine the phrase’s meaning.
reason: Both identify uncertainty created by clause (iv)’s “reasonably likely” standard, although the proposed issue frames it as speculative and insufficiently tied to a line of business, while g1 frames it as lexical vagueness or ambiguity. The proposed issue’s separate objection to clause (ii)’s hiring bar has no counterpart in g1.

issue: "Any and all services provided by Licensee in connection with or relating to the operation" of the facilities is unbounded, and "relating to" would sweep in services having only a loose connection to the licensed facilities. The clause also miscites the defined term ("Hard Rock Hotei/Casinos").
gold_issue: The broad definition of “Licensed Services” as services provided “in connection with or relating to” hotel operations was disputed as to whether it encompassed the Rehab television program rather than excluding it as an independent entertainment product.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue principally concerns “any and all services” and “in connection with or relating to the operation,” while separately flagging “Hard Rock Hotei/Casinos” as an apparent typo. Candidate g1 concerns the same scope language—especially “in connection with or relating to”—and whether it reaches the Rehab television program.
evidence: “Licensed Services” is defined broadly to include “any and all services provided by [the Hard Rock Defendants] in connection with or relating to the operation of [the Hotel].” (Agreement ¶ 1(1) (emphasis added).) Because Rehab portrays a party at the Hotel, it relates to the Hotel’s services.
reason: Both identify the breadth of “in connection with or relating to” as creating an expansive scope: the proposed issue describes loose connections generally, while g1 applies that breadth to whether the Rehab program is covered. The proposed issue’s additional complaint about “Hotei/Casinos” is separate and is not addressed by g1.

issue: The worldwide carve-out permitting "promotion, advertising or marketing (not including the sale of merchandise) and broadcasting of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos" does not define what counts as broadcasting or promotion "of" the licensed facilities. Programming or media exploitation bearing the marks but going beyond advertising the facility falls in a zone the words do not resolve.
gold_issue: The authorization for “promotion, advertising or marketing” and “broadcasting” was disputed as to whether it encompassed Rehab or left the program unauthorized as an entertainment product.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the worldwide carve-out for “promotion, advertising or marketing” and “broadcasting” of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos, particularly what “of” and those activities encompass. Candidate g1 concerns those same words and whether they cover Rehab; g2 instead concerns the separate term “exclusive license” and whether it restricts other Hard Rock-branded ventures.
evidence: HRCI also asserts that Rehab is an unauthorized “entertainment product” and beyond the scope of the Arbitration Clause. (PI. Opp’n at 22.) However, the Agreement permits the Hard Rock Defendants to use the Hard Rock Marks “in connection with the ... promotion of Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos and Hard Rock Casinos.” (Agreement ¶ 2(a) (emphasis added); see also ¶ 4(a).) This “promotion, advertising or marketing ... and broadcasting” may be done “anywhere in the world.” (Agreement ¶ 2(a).)
reason: The proposed issue and g1 identify the same interpretive boundary: whether a marked television or entertainment program falls within the worldwide authorization for promotion and broadcasting of the licensed facilities or is an unauthorized entertainment product. The proposed issue states the problem generally, while g1 applies it specifically to Rehab.

issue: The grant of an "exclusive license" in the Morton Territories cannot be squared with Section 3(a), which gives Licensor "the right to the use and exploitation of the Hard Rock Hotel Marks anywhere in the world for a Hotel facility that does not include a Casino", excepting only Nevada. The two provisions both purport to control use of the Hotel Marks inside the Territories.
gold_issue: The term “exclusive license” was disputed as meaning either only that HRCI could not license the Hard Rock Hotel and Casino Marks or compete in their licensed use, or that HRCI could not compete through other Hard Rock-branded products and ventures in the Morton Territories.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “exclusive license” in Section 2(a) and its asserted conflict with Section 3(a)’s reservation allowing Licensor to use the Hotel Marks for a Hotel without a Casino outside Nevada. Candidate g1 concerns the separate authorization for “promotion, advertising or marketing” and “broadcasting”; g2 concerns “exclusive license,” the limiting words “only” and “solely,” and Section 3(a)’s reservation of uses outside the specifically licensed Hotel/Casino field.
evidence: The Hard Rock Defendants argue that the term “exclusive license” means HRCI cannot compete with the Hard Rock Defendants “with respect to the particular products or particular territories for which the exclusive license was granted.” (Defs’ Opp’n at 5.). But no provision in the Agreement prohibits HRCI from opening other Hard Rock branded ventures such as restaurants and music venues in the Morton Territories. The Agreement only forbids HRCI from developing Hotel/Casinos in the Morton territories and Hotels in Nevada. (See Agreement ¶ 3(a).)
reason: Both defects concern whether “exclusive license,” read with Section 3(a), excludes HRCI only from the specifically licensed Hotel/Casino uses or also from other Hard Rock-branded uses within the Morton Territories. The proposed issue focuses specifically on non-casino Hotels, while g2 states the broader dispute over other products and ventures, so it is the same underlying problem framed more narrowly.

issue: The quality benchmark — "good quality at least as high as the quality of similar goods presently sold ... by Licensee" at the Las Vegas facility — is self-referential and fixed to an unrecorded baseline, and "equal to and commensurate with" adds no measurable standard. What quality failure would breach the clause cannot be determined from its words.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “good quality at least as high as the quality of similar goods presently sold” and “equal to and commensurate with,” alleging that those benchmarks lack an ascertainable baseline or measurable standard. Candidate g1 concerns the scope of “nature and quality,” specifically whether “quality” covers only degree of excellence or also content, character, services, and customer experience.
reason: The proposed issue challenges the indeterminacy of the comparative quality benchmarks, whereas g1 concerns what kinds of characteristics fall within “nature and quality.” These are distinct defects despite both involving quality.

issue: Arbitration is confined to disputes "regarding the failure of Licensee to conform to any provision of quality control as set forth herein", but the contract never identifies which provisions are quality-control provisions. "Any substantial failure ... in any respect" and the misused word "proscribed" (for prescribed) add further uncertainty about the trigger and the selection process.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “provision of quality control as set forth herein” and the alleged silence identifying such provisions, plus “any substantial failure ... in any respect” and “proscribed.” Candidate g1 turns on “any dispute,” “provision of quality control,” and especially the meaning and reach of “quality” as applied to Rehab’s content and the character and services of the Tulsa and Albuquerque properties.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the agreement fails to identify which contractual provisions qualify as quality-control provisions, with additional uncertainty from “any substantial failure ... in any respect” and “proscribed.” Candidate g1 instead concerns whether particular objections about content and property character fall within “quality” or “quality control,” so it identifies a different scope dispute rather than the alleged missing identification.

issue: The exclusion of "any claims or controversies not specifically identified hereinabove" from arbitration depends entirely on what 5(a) is taken to have specifically identified, and 5(a)'s reference to "any provision of quality control as set forth herein" is itself unspecified. A mixed dispute — quality failure alleged alongside trademark validity — cannot be allocated between the two clauses.
gold_issue: The exclusion for disputes relating to the Agreement’s “validity” or the “validity or enforceability” of trademark rights was disputed as to whether claims pleaded as trademark infringement or as breaches warranting termination fell within that exclusion despite having quality-control factual underpinnings.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “any claims or controversies not specifically identified hereinabove,” its cross-reference to 5(a)’s “any provision of quality control as set forth herein,” and the exclusion for trademark-validity disputes. Candidate g1 turns on “validity of this License Agreement” and “validity or enforceability of any trademark rights hereunder,” read against the quality-control arbitration language, and asks how claims combining those characterizations and quality-control facts are allocated.
evidence:
However, “disputes relating to the validity of [the] License Agreement or the validity or enforceability of any trademark rights hereunder, shall be excluded from arbitration.” (Agreement ¶ 5(d).)
HRCI argues that claims relating to Rehab and the Tulsa and Albuquerque Properties are exempt from arbitration because they concern trademark infringement and contractual breaches warranting termination of the Agreement. In deciding whether a dispute falls within an arbitration clause, courts must “focus on the factual allegations in the complaint rather than the legal causes of action asserted.”
reason: Both identify the boundary between quality-control disputes assigned to arbitration and trademark-validity or termination disputes excluded from it. The proposed issue frames that boundary as an inability to allocate mixed disputes caused by the cross-references, while g1 frames it as deciding whether trademark-labelled claims with quality-control factual underpinnings fall within the exclusion, so the underlying problem is the same but not stated identically.

issue: "Best efforts" is undefined and the clause supplies no benchmark, cost ceiling or required action against which either party's protective efforts could be measured. It is also mutual and open-ended, so what protection either owes is indeterminate.
gold_issue: The obligation to use “best efforts” to protect the marks and goodwill was challenged as too vague to enforce because it allegedly supplied no objective criteria applicable to a reality-show genre that did not exist when the Agreement was executed.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “use their best efforts to protect” and the clause’s silence about benchmarks, costs, and required protective actions. Candidate g1 concerns the same “best efforts” language and the alleged absence of objective criteria for measuring those efforts, particularly in relation to a reality-show genre that did not exist when the Agreement was signed.
evidence: The Hard Rock Defendants contend that there are no objective criteria to measure “best efforts” because “the genre of reality shows like ‘Rehab’ did not even exist” when the Agreement was executed.
reason: Both identify the same defect: the “best efforts” obligation allegedly lacks objective criteria by which performance can be measured. The proposed issue adds concerns about mutuality, open-endedness, and the absence of a cost ceiling, while g1 contextualizes the missing benchmark through the later-created reality-show genre, but these are variations on the same core complaint.

issue: The cross-promotion duty applies only "when practical and appropriate", a standard with no benchmark and no decision-maker named. Whether a party ever breaches by omitting the other's facilities cannot be determined from the clause.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “when practical and appropriate” and the clause’s silence about a benchmark or decision-maker for that standard. Candidate g1 concerns the word “locations,” specifically whether it means places where both parties maintain facilities or the geographic reach of the promotional material.
reason: The proposed issue challenges the undefined standard governing whether cross-promotion is required, whereas g1 identifies competing meanings of “locations” that determine which advertisements or geographic places are covered. These are distinct defects involving different words.

issue: The table-tent display Licensor must place in its own restaurants referencing Licensee's facilities must be "reasonably acceptable to Licensor", which appears to be a mechanical error for Licensee and leaves the obligor as the sole judge of its own performance. As written the sentence gives Licensor an approval right over material it alone supplies.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “reasonably acceptable to Licensor” in the table-tent sentence and the resulting self-approval right. Candidate g1 turns on “locations” in the opening sentence—whether it means places where both parties maintain facilities or the geographic reach of the advertising.
reason: The proposed issue concerns Licensor’s apparent power to approve the promotional display it must itself supply, whereas g1 concerns the geographic meaning of “locations.” These are distinct alleged defects in different language of the provision.

issue: Licensor's right to develop web pages for "other Hard Rock Facilities as they may develop" cannot be squared with the exclusive license to the Hotel and Casino Marks in the Morton Territories granted by Section 2(a), since Hard Rock Facilities include Licensee's Hotel/Casinos. The Licensee-only carve-out for the Territories and the Internet sales rules in 2(b)(v) leave the boundary of each party's web rights contested.
gold_issue: The exception allowing the Licensee to “develop, maintain and update a Web page” was disputed as to whether it both limited HRCI’s website rights and encompassed an exclusive right to register hardrockcasinoalbuquerque.com.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “other Hard Rock Facilities as they may develop,” the exception permitting Licensee to develop pages for Hotel/Casinos or Casinos in the Morton Territories, and their interaction with Sections 2(a) and 2(b)(v). G1 concerns that same exception and “develop, maintain and update a Web page” as applied to exclusive domain registration; g2 concerns only the singular “a Web page”; g3 concerns “other party’s Web pages” in the linking sentence.
evidence: The use of the word “except” limits HRCI’s ability to develop, maintain and update websites for Hotel/Casinos and Casinos in the Morton Territories. Additionally, the language “developing], maintaining], and updating] a Web page” is reasonably capable of encompassing the Hard Rock Defendants’ right to register this domain name. The Agreement is therefore ambiguous as to whether it granted the Hard Rock Defendants an exclusive right to register hardrockcasinoalbuquerque.com.
reason: The proposed issue and g1 both concern whether the “except” clause limits Licensor’s web rights in the Morton Territories and gives Licensee exclusivity there. The proposed issue frames the conflict broadly through Sections 2(a) and 2(b)(v), while g1 addresses the narrower claimed exclusive right to register a particular domain name.

issue: The unrestricted right to "sublicense or franchise any or all of the rights and licenses granted hereunder" cannot easily be squared with the first-offer right in Section 9(c), since a sublicense of all rights would transfer the business without triggering negotiation with Licensor. Nothing in either clause says which governs a wholesale sublicense.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “sublicense or franchise any or all of the rights and licenses granted hereunder,” together with the provision’s silence about its priority relative to Section 9(c)’s first-offer right. Candidate g1 turns on the same quoted grant but asks whether “rights and licenses granted hereunder” encompass use of the unaltered Hard Rock Marks at the Tulsa and Albuquerque properties, not whether a wholesale sublicense circumvents Section 9(c).
reason: Although both focus on the sublicense grant, they identify different defects. The proposed issue alleges an unresolved conflict with Section 9(c)’s first-offer right for a wholesale transfer, while g1 concerns whether the granted rights substantively include use of unaltered marks at two properties.

clause_name: Limitation of Lincoln General’s lawsuit claims
issue: The paragraph is framed as a limitation ("agrees to limit the scope of its claims ... to the following") but each enumerated category is opened up again by catch-alls — "This includes, but is not limited to," "among other things," and "other persons or entities" — so the general language arguably swallows the enumerated specifics. A court would have to decide whether ejusdem generis confines the retained claims to the listed IBNR-commission and improper-payment theories.
gold_issue: The open-ended phrases “includes, but is not limited to,” “by Defendants and/or other persons or entities,” and “among other things” were disputed as to whether the letter’s delineation was exhaustive or broad enough to encompass claims not specifically listed.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “agrees to limit the scope of its claims ... to the following” in tension with “includes, but is not limited to,” “among other things,” and “other persons or entities.” Candidate g1 concerns those same open-ended phrases and whether they make the letter non-exhaustive and broad enough to encompass unlisted claims.
evidence: Furthermore, the language of the April 30, 2008 letter itself is broad, using language such as “includes, but is not limited to,” “by Defendants and/or other persons or entities,” and “such claims may encompass actions seeking legal or equitable relief for, among other things, .... ” (Id. (emphasis added)).
reason: Both identify the same defect: the provision purports to limit the claims to enumerated categories, yet its open-ended phrases may broaden the retained claims beyond those specifically listed. The proposed issue adds ejusdem generis as a possible interpretive method, but that does not materially change the defect.

clause_name: Limitation of Lincoln General’s lawsuit claims
issue: Category (2) (paying or overpaying claims on policies not reinsured or only partially reinsured, out of a Lincoln General-funded account) overlaps with the claims excluded by the "Other Causes of Action" paragraph, which bars claims for "mishandling of insurance claims on the reinsured policies." Which paragraph governs a claim that sounds in both is not resolved.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on Category (2)’s coverage of payments from a Lincoln General-funded account for policies not or only partially reinsured, in alleged conflict with the “Other Causes of Action” bar for “mishandling of insurance claims on the reinsured policies.” Candidate g1 turns on “includes, but is not limited to,” “by Defendants and/or other persons or entities,” and “among other things,” and whether those phrases expand the delineated claims beyond those specifically listed.
reason: The proposed issue alleges an unresolved conflict between Category (2) and the separate “Other Causes of Action” exclusion. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether open-ended wording makes the letter’s claim delineation non-exhaustive, so it names a different defect.

issue: The tolling runs "for five (5) years of until all claims ... have been paid and settled," where the mangled conjunction leaves it unclear whether the period is five years, or until all claims are paid, or the longer or shorter of the two. "[P]aid and settled ... pursuant to any and all agreements between them" also fixes no ascertainable end date.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “for five (5) years of until all claims ... have been paid and settled” and “pursuant to any and all agreements between them,” particularly the ambiguous conjunction and indeterminate endpoint. Candidate g1 concerns “or otherwise related to,” specifically whether that phrase covers additional existing claims or only claims arising while the MOU was in force.
reason: The proposed issue challenges the uncertainty in the tolling period’s duration and endpoint. Candidate g1 instead concerns which causes of action fall within the tolling provision, so it records a different defect.

issue: The provision incorporates the "Other Causes of Action" defined in "the April 28, 2008 letter agreement," but the letter agreement in the record is dated April 30, 2008. The misdescription puts in issue which document, and hence which definition, is being incorporated.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the cross-reference to “the April 28, 2008 letter agreement” and its conflict with the record’s April 30 letter. Candidate g1 turns on “shall extend to, but not be limited to” and whether those words cover claims beyond the letter’s specified Other Causes of Action.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the incorrect date misidentifies the incorporated letter. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether the phrase “shall extend to, but not be limited to” expands tolling beyond the claims specified in the referenced letter; it does not record the date discrepancy as a defect.

issue: The April 2008 letter tolls the Other Causes of Action "until the Lawsuit has been settled or otherwise finally resolved, including the completion of any appeals," while section VI tolls them for five years or until all claims are paid. Which tolling term governs those causes of action after the Lawsuit's dismissal cannot be answered from either document alone.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the cross-reference to the April 2008 letter and the allegedly conflicting tolling endpoints in that letter and section VI. Candidate g1 turns on “shall extend to, but not be limited to” and whether those words encompass claims beyond those specified in the letter or original suit.
reason: The proposed issue concerns a conflict between two tolling durations and uncertainty over which termination event governs the referenced Other Causes of Action. Candidate g1 instead concerns the substantive scope of claims covered by “shall extend to, but not be limited to,” so it names a different defect.

clause_name: Xk. Failure to complete required actions
issue: The heading covers "Failure to Complete the Required Actions ... or Later Breach," but the operative text addresses only the parties being "not able to complete" the contemplated documents and says nothing about breach. Whether refiling is also the remedy for a later breach, and whether it is an exclusive remedy at all, is left open.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the heading’s words “or Later Breach,” the operative sentence’s silence about later breach, and the remedy language insofar as it may or may not make refiling exclusive. Candidate g1 turns on “Lincoln’s sole remedy shall be to refile the lawsuit” and whether “the lawsuit” limits a later action to claims asserted in the original 2007 suit.
reason: No candidate names the proposed heading/operative-text mismatch or the uncertainty whether refiling applies to later breach and is exclusive. Candidate g1 instead concerns which claims may be included when Lincoln refiles, a distinct question about the scope of the successive lawsuit.

clause_name: Xk. Failure to complete required actions
issue: Limiting Lincoln General's remedy to refiling the lawsuit cannot be squared with section V's agreement that the Memorandum is "sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement," nor with the unconditional payment duty in section IV. A court must decide whether section IX displaces enforcement of the Memorandum.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “Lincoln’s [sole] remedy shall be to refile the lawsuit” and its asserted conflict with Section V’s enforcement language and Section IV’s payment duty. Candidate g1 concerns the same remedy phrase but asks whether “refile the lawsuit” restricts the claims in the new suit to the original 2007 claims, particularly in light of the dismissal and tolling provisions.
reason: Although both concern the limitation stating that Lincoln’s remedy is to refile, they identify different defects. The proposed issue asks whether that remedy displaces enforcement and payment rights under Sections V and IV, whereas g1 concerns only whether a refiled suit is limited to claims asserted in the 2007 action.

issue: The recital that Lender "has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage" under the work-out arrangement conflicts with Attachment A paragraph b, which states the aggregate Plan payments will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage and that the account will remain delinquent. A borrower could argue the recital states the bargain's purpose and controls the operative payment schedule.
gold_issue: The recital that Aurora “has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage” created whole-contract tension with Attachment A’s statement that the Plan payments would be insufficient to pay the arrearage, leaving Aurora’s repayment obligation ambiguous when the agreement was read as a whole.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage” and its conflict with Attachment A paragraph b’s statement that aggregate Plan payments will be insufficient and leave the account delinquent. Candidate g1 concerns the same recital language and the same conflicting Attachment A statement.
evidence: Although it is true that Attachment A discloses that the “aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage,” Aurora never reconciles this provision with the recital that Aurora “has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement^]”
reason: Both identify the same contradiction between the recital’s promise to allow repayment of the arrearage and Attachment A’s statement that the Plan payments will not fully repay it. The proposed issue adds that the recital could control as a statement of purpose, while g1 frames the resulting problem as whole-contract ambiguity, but this is the same underlying defect.

issue: "[F]orbear from exercising any or all of its rights and remedies" is ambiguous as to whether Lender must forbear from all remedies or may elect which ones to forbear from. The disjunctive "any or all" gives the borrower's principal protection no fixed content.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the internal wording “any or all of its rights and remedies” and the scope of the required forbearance. Candidate g1 turns on the forbearance promise as a whole in conflict with the recital and Attachment A language stating that Aurora would allow repayment of the arrearage.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether “any or all” lets the lender choose which remedies to forbear from. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether the forbearance promise was Aurora’s sole obligation despite separate language requiring it to allow repayment of the arrearage, so it identifies a different defect.

issue: The forbearance promise cannot be squared with paragraph 8, which states that a commenced foreclosure "will not be withdrawn," and with paragraph 7's declaration that nothing herein waives any right to commence or resume foreclosure. What Lender actually gave up during the plan term is the very thing those provisions take back.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns paragraph 3’s promise to “forbear from exercising any or all of its rights and remedies,” as allegedly conflicting with paragraph 7’s nonwaiver of foreclosure rights and paragraph 8’s statement that a commenced foreclosure “will not be withdrawn.” Candidate g1 concerns the same forbearance promise but compares it to the recital and Attachment A language stating that Aurora agreed to allow repayment of the arrearage and that the plan was implemented for that purpose.
reason: The proposed issue alleges that the forbearance promise is taken back by paragraphs 7 and 8’s preservation of foreclosure rights. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether treating forbearance as Aurora’s sole obligation can be reconciled with separate language promising an opportunity to repay the arrearage; that is a different contractual conflict.

issue: The First Plan payment is due "on or before 11/18/2009," but the effectiveness condition in Attachment A requires Lender to receive that payment by the Agreement Return Date of 11/15/2009, and the cover letter demands it by 11/15/2009. A payment made on the date this provision allows would fail the condition another provision imposes.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “on or before 11/18/2009” and its conflict with the 11/15/2009 Agreement Return Date and cover-letter deadline. Candidate g1 turns on “[f]or the purposes of repayment of the Arrearage” and its conflict with Attachment A’s statement that the payments “will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage.”
reason: The proposed issue identifies a conflict between the First Plan payment deadline and separate effectiveness/cover-letter deadlines. Candidate g1 instead identifies a contradiction between the stated purpose of repaying the arrearage and the disclosure that the plan payments would be insufficient to do so; these are different defects.

clause_name: Attachment A b Plan Payment Insufficiency
issue: The statement that the aggregate Plan payments will be insufficient and the account will remain delinquent conflicts with the recital that Lender agreed to allow Customer "to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement" and with paragraph 4's reference to full reinstatement. A court would have to decide what the plan was for if it could never cure the default.
gold_issue: The statement that the “aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage” supported Aurora’s denial of any repayment obligation but created whole-contract tension with the recital and payment-purpose clause stating that the arrangement was for repayment of the arrearage.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage” and “Customer's account will remain delinquent,” as conflicting with the recital’s promise to allow repayment and paragraph 4’s full-reinstatement language. Candidate g1 concerns the same insufficiency sentence, specifically its conflict with the repayment recital and the separate clause stating that the Plan’s purpose was repayment of the arrearage.
evidence: Although it is true that Attachment A discloses that the “aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage,” Aurora never reconciles this provision with the recital that Aurora “has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement^]” Nor does Aurora explain the first clause in the Attachment, which specifies that the payment plan is being implemented “[f]or the purposes of repayment of the Arrearage^]”
reason: Both identify the contradiction between Attachment A’s statement that the Plan payments cannot cure the arrearage and the agreement’s language presenting the workout as a means of repaying that arrearage. The proposed issue additionally invokes continued delinquency and paragraph 4’s reinstatement language, while g1 emphasizes the recital and payment-purpose clause, but these are closely overlapping formulations of the same defect.

issue: The final clause is garbled beyond sense ("the terms of this reement ae conzartunl an not 8 mere rsa"), so the words meant to declare the terms contractual and not a mere recital cannot be read. That mechanical corruption of the integration clause's operative language is itself a matter for construction.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the garbled final clause, “the terms of this reement ae conzartunl an not 8 mere rsa.” Candidate g1 concerns “no promise or inducement or agreement not herein expressed” and “this Release contains the entire agreement,” specifically whether those words constitute a merger clause despite omitting conventional merger terminology.
reason: The proposed issue alleges mechanical corruption that makes the final clause unreadable. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether the preceding complete-agreement language functions as a merger clause excluding prior oral agreements, so it names a different defect.

issue: Confidentiality is owed to every "person not party or privy to this settlement," and "privy" is undefined, while the added bar on terms being "used to the detriment of the Parties" has no stated measure of detriment. Both terms would need construction before any breach could be found.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “person not party or privy to this settlement,” particularly undefined “privy,” and on “used to the detriment of the Parties,” particularly the absence of a measure of detriment. Candidate g1 instead turns on “the terms of this Release and the terms of the settlement of this claim” and whether that phrase covers only written contractual provisions or also oral conditions and the underlying actions’ facts and existence.
reason: The proposed issue challenges uncertainty in who is “privy” and what constitutes “detriment,” whereas g1 concerns what information is encompassed by “the terms of this Release and the terms of the settlement of this claim.” These are distinct alleged defects involving different words.

issue: The condition covers representations "set forth or incorporated by reference in this Insurance Agreement", which by Section 2.01(n) means every representation in every Operative Document, without any materiality qualifier. How far the incorporation reaches for purposes of this closing condition is not stated here.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “set forth or incorporated by reference in this Insurance Agreement,” including the alleged cross-reference through Section 2.01(n), and the silence about the reach of that incorporation and any materiality limitation. Candidate g1 turns on “shall be true and correct on and as of the Closing Date” and the consequences and proof of a material breach of that requirement, particularly increased risk of loss versus causation of a HELOC default.
reason: The proposed issue concerns uncertainty over which representations are incorporated into the closing condition and thus must be true. Candidate g1 instead concerns how material breach of that condition may be proved—by increased risk of loss without showing that the breach caused a HELOC default—so it identifies a different defect.

issue: The trigger states two different thresholds in one sentence: a breach "which materially and adversely affects the value of the interests of the Purchaser, the Noteholders, the Indenture Trustee or the Note Insurer ... or which adversely affects the interests of the Note Insurer." Whether the Note Insurer must show materiality at all, having been named in both limbs, is squarely presented by the words.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the contrast between “materially and adversely affects the value of the interests of ... the Note Insurer” and “or which adversely affects the interests of the Note Insurer.” g1 turns on the meaning of “adversely affects the interests of the Note Insurer”—increased risk versus actual harm through default—while g2 turns on the provision’s silence about any requirement that a breach cause default, considered against the I&I and SSA provisions.
reason: Neither candidate addresses whether the Note Insurer must satisfy materiality because it appears in both trigger limbs. Both instead concern whether an adverse effect requires an actual loan default or existing harm, so they identify a different defect.

issue: Cure, repurchase or substitution is made "the sole and exclusive remedy," yet Section 2.02(n) of the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement independently obliges the Sponsor to defend and indemnify the Insurer against all losses arising from the same breach of this Section 7. Whether the sole-remedy clause caps the Insurer's recovery under the Insurance Agreement is the central relational question of this transaction.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “sole and exclusive remedy under this Agreement or otherwise,” its Section 13 indemnity exception, and their relationship to I&I § 2.02(n). Candidate g1 turns on “adversely affects the interests of the Note Insurer”; candidate g2 turns on Section 7’s silence about any requirement that a breach cause a HELOC default, considered alongside the I&I Event-of-Default and SSA repurchase provisions.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether Section 7’s sole-and-exclusive-remedy sentence limits a separate I&I indemnity obligation. Neither candidate records that defect: g1 construes the adverse-effect trigger, while g2 addresses whether Section 7 silently requires a loan default before repurchase remedies become available.

clause_name: Section 2.05(a). Opinion for substitutions and repurchases
issue: The Opinion of Counsel condition applies only to a HELOC "that is not in default or as to which default is not reasonably foreseeable", and neither "default" nor "reasonably foreseeable" is given any measure here. Whether a given delinquent HELOC falls inside or outside the condition is therefore contestable.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the undefined words “default” and “reasonably foreseeable” in “not in default or as to which default is not reasonably foreseeable.” Candidate g1 turns on the same conditional sentence, but specifically on its recognition of repurchase or substitution for a HELOC that is not yet in default, rather than on uncertainty over what counts as default or reasonable foreseeability.
reason: Although both concern the nondefault language, they identify different issues. The proposed issue alleges uncertainty in deciding whether a delinquent HELOC is in default or foreseeably headed for default, while g1 construes the provision as confirming that repurchase may occur before any loan default; it does not identify ambiguity in those thresholds.

issue: The condition is numbered 5.14, the same number carried later by the Self-Insured Retention condition, so the cross-reference in Condition 5.7 to "Condition 5.14" is ambiguous. The duplication is on the face of the numbering.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the heading number “5.14,” its duplication for the Self-Insured Retention condition, and Condition 5.7’s cross-reference to “Condition 5.14.” Candidate g1 concerns “all claims and disputes will be litigated” and whether it unambiguously selects New York; g2 concerns that New York forum requirement’s conflict with the Service of Suit Endorsement permitting the insured to choose a court.
reason: Neither candidate addresses the duplicated condition number or the resulting ambiguity in Condition 5.7’s cross-reference. The candidates instead concern the substantive forum-selection language, either standing alone or in conflict with the Service of Suit Endorsement.

issue: This condition requires that "all claims and disputes will be litigated in the Supreme Court of the State of New York ... or in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York," which cannot be squared with the Service of Suit endorsement, under which the Insurer agrees at the Insured's request to submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction within the United States. Which controls the forum for a California insured is the plain point of conflict.
gold_issue: The New York forum requirement was in whole-contract tension with the Service of Suit Endorsement’s promise to submit to a court chosen by the insured, requiring the court to determine whether the endorsement modified the original forum-selection clause.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “all claims and disputes will be litigated” in the specified New York courts as conflicting with the Service of Suit Endorsement’s submission to any competent U.S. court. Candidate g1 concerns only whether the New York designation is ambiguous in isolation, while g2 concerns that exact conflict and whether the endorsement modifies the New York forum requirement.
evidence: Accordingly, the Court finds that upon interpreting the Policy as a whole, the Service of Suit Endorsement modified the forum selection clause so that the plain language of the Policy unambiguously permits Plaintiff to bring suit in a forum of its choosing.
reason: The proposed issue and g2 identify the same conflict between the mandatory New York forum language and the endorsement allowing the insured to choose any competent U.S. court. Both ask which provision controls, so g2 is a direct match.

issue: The clause submits to the Insured's chosen court and then reserves the Insurer's rights "to remove an action ... or to seek a transfer of a case to another court," so it is ambiguous whether it confers a forum choice at all or merely waives objections to personal jurisdiction. The two sentences point in opposite directions.
gold_issue: The reservation of Starr’s right “to seek a transfer” was susceptible to competing facial readings—whether it curtailed TriUnion’s initial forum choice or merely preserved Starr’s right to request transfer after suit was filed.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the interaction between “at your request will submit to the jurisdiction” and the reservation “to remove an action” or “to seek a transfer.” g1 concerns the meaning of the submission promise alone; g2 concerns whether the transfer reservation curtails that initial choice or only applies after filing; g3 concerns the Service of Suit language’s conflict with the separate New York forum-selection clause.
evidence: Here, the additional clause cited by Defendant does exactly that — it simply reserves Defendant’s right to seek removal or transfer of a case to a different forum after Plaintiff files suit in its chosen forum. It does not, however, alter or change Plaintiffs ability to choose the forum in the first place.
reason: The proposed issue and g2 identify the same apparent conflict between the insured’s initial forum choice and the insurer’s reserved removal or transfer rights. The proposed issue is slightly broader because it includes removal and characterizes the alternative as merely consenting to personal jurisdiction, while g2 focuses on transfer and its timing.

issue: The Insurer's agreement to "submit to the jurisdiction of a court of competent jurisdiction within the United States" at the Insured's request cannot be squared with Condition 5.10, which requires that all claims and disputes be litigated in the New York Supreme Court for New York County or the Southern District of New York. Whether the endorsement supersedes or merely supplements the forum clause is the central relational question.
gold_issue: The Service of Suit promise was in whole-contract tension with the original New York forum-selection clause, requiring the court to decide whether the endorsement modified that clause to permit suit in TriUnion’s chosen forum.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “at your request will submit to the jurisdiction of a court of competent jurisdiction within the United States” in conflict with Condition 5.10’s New York forum requirement. Candidate g1 concerns the meaning of that submission phrase by itself; g2 concerns the reservation “to seek a transfer”; and g3 concerns the same submission phrase in relation to the original New York forum-selection clause and whether the endorsement modified that clause.
evidence: Accordingly, the Court finds that upon interpreting the Policy as a whole, the Service of Suit Endorsement modified the forum selection clause so that the plain language of the Policy unambiguously permits Plaintiff to bring suit in a forum of its choosing.
reason: The proposed issue and g3 identify the same conflict between the Service of Suit promise allowing the insured to select a competent U.S. court and the original clause designating New York, and both ask whether the endorsement changed the original forum restriction. Their formulations differ only slightly: the proposal says “supersedes or merely supplements,” while g3 says “modified.”

issue: "All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged" would preserve Condition 5.10's New York forum clause, which the body of this same Service of Suit endorsement contradicts. Which sentence yields — the saving clause or the undertaking above it — is exactly what a court would be asked to decide.
gold_issue: The statement that “[a]ll other terms and conditions” remained unchanged posed a whole-contract coherence question over whether the preceding Service of Suit terms changed the original forum-selection clause or left it intact.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged,” especially “other” and “remain unchanged,” in relation to the preceding Service of Suit undertaking and Condition 5.10’s New York forum clause. Candidate g1 concerns the same saving-clause words and the same question whether the preceding endorsement terms changed that forum-selection clause or left it intact.
evidence: On the same page and immediately following the Service of Suit provision discussed above, the Endorsement further states: “All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged.” By specifying that “other terms and conditions ... remain unchanged,” the Endorsement further demonstrates that the terms and conditions listed directly above — including “we, at your request will submit to the jurisdiction of a court of competent jurisdiction within the United States” — in fact changed the original insurance agreement.
reason: Both identify the same interpretive defect: whether the saving clause leaves the original New York forum-selection clause intact despite the preceding Service of Suit undertaking, or instead confirms that the undertaking modified it. The candidate frames this as whole-contract coherence, but it is the same conflict over which terms remain unchanged.

issue: Paragraph 1 commits "any controversy or claim arising out of or relating to your employment relationship" to binding arbitration, which cannot be reconciled with the Claims Not Covered clause (c008) excluding workers' compensation, unemployment, NLRA, EEOC, equitable-relief and benefit-plan claims. A court would have to decide how far "any" is cut back by that exclusion list.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “any controversy or claim” and its asserted conflict with the separate Claims Not Covered clause’s express exclusions. Candidate g1 turns on the same broad introductory phrase but alleges a different problem: the silence created by not expressly naming RICRA, FEPA, and CRPDA despite general references to discrimination and state-law claims.
reason: The proposed issue concerns how an express exclusion clause limits the word “any,” whereas g1 concerns whether unlisted statutory claims nevertheless fall within the provision’s general inclusive language. Those are distinct defects involving different contractual text, even though both address claim scope.

issue: The covered-claims list is introduced by "Includes, but is not limited to" and closed by the catch-all "claims for violation of any federal, state, or other governmental law," so the enumerated specifics give no boundary to the class. The internal qualifier "tort claims (not otherwise exluded)" compounds this by referring outward without identifying what is excluded.
gold_issue: The combination of “including but not limited to” enumerated discrimination claims and the catch-all covering violations of “any ... state ... statute” presented a general-versus-specific/list-scope question whether the unenumerated RICRA, FEPA, and CRPDA claims were covered.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “Includes, but is not limited to,” the catch-all “claims for violation of any federal, state, or other governmental law,” and separately “tort claims (not otherwise exluded).” Candidate g1 turns on the first two features plus the provision’s silence as to RICRA, FEPA, and CRPDA; it does not address the tort-claim exclusion cross-reference.
evidence: “A party cannot avoid arbitration ... because the arbitration clause uses general, inclusive language, rather than listing every possible specific claim.”
reason: Both identify the list-scope problem created by general inclusive language and the catch-all: whether claims omitted from the enumeration remain covered. Alignment is partial because g1 focuses specifically on omitted RICRA, FEPA, and CRPDA claims, while the proposed issue makes a broader boundarylessness complaint and adds a separate concern about the unidentified exclusions for tort claims.

issue: This clause expressly covers "violations of confidentiality or breaches of trade secrets," but c008 carves out claims for injunctive or equitable relief "including without limitation claims for unfair competition and the use or unauthorized disclosure of trade secrets or confidential information." The same trade-secret claim is thus both covered and not covered.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “violations of confidentiality or breaches of trade secrets” and its alleged conflict with c008’s carve-out for equitable relief involving trade secrets or confidential information. Candidate g1 turns on the discrimination list introduced by “including but not limited to,” the catch-all “any ... state ... statute,” and the omission of the names RICRA, FEPA, and CRPDA.
reason: The proposed issue alleges an internal conflict between coverage of trade-secret/confidentiality claims and a separate equitable-relief carve-out. Candidate g1 instead concerns whether general discrimination and state-statute language covers claims under statutes not expressly named, so it identifies a different defect.

issue: The equitable-relief carve-out opens mutually ("A claim by you or us for injunctive or other equitable relief") but closes unilaterally ("for which we may seek and obtain relief from a court of competent jurisdiction"), so it is unclear whether the employee too may go to court. The surrounding list markers are also garbled ("L", "Iv.", "_A claim"), leaving the enumeration's structure uncertain.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on the contrast between “A claim by you or us” and “for which we may seek and obtain relief,” plus the list markers “L”, “Iv.”, and “_A claim.” Candidate g1 turns on whether “[a] claim before the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission” remains excluded after Commission proceedings terminate, while g2 turns on whether “[a] claim ... for injunctive or other equitable relief” excludes a whole mixed-remedy action or only its equitable-relief component.
reason: Neither candidate records the proposed defect. Although g2 concerns the same equitable-relief carve-out, it addresses the division of mixed legal and equitable remedies between arbitration and court, not the pronoun mismatch allegedly making court access unilateral; neither candidate addresses the garbled enumeration.

issue: The exclusion of "a claim before the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (or agency with concurrent jurisdiction)" cannot be squared with c007, which commits discrimination claims and "any claim that could be asserted ... before an administrative agency" to arbitration. A court would be asked which governs a statutory discrimination claim.
gold_issue: The lexical scope of “[a] claim before the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (or agency with concurrent jurisdiction)” was disputed as to whether the exclusion continued after a right-to-sue letter terminated Commission proceedings or applied only while the claim remained before the Commission.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “[a] claim before the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (or agency with concurrent jurisdiction)” together with c007’s coverage of discrimination claims and claims assertable before an administrative agency. g1 turns specifically on the word “before” and whether that exclusion survives a right-to-sue letter; g2 instead concerns “[a] claim ... for injunctive or other equitable relief” and mixed remedies.
evidence: Once Plaintiff received his right to sue letter, his claim before the Commission was voluntarily terminated, therefore Plaintiffs claim was no longer before the Commission.
reason: Both identify uncertainty over whether an EEOC-filed discrimination claim is excluded from arbitration. The proposed issue frames this broadly as a conflict with c007’s arbitration coverage, while g1 identifies the narrower temporal question that resolves the overlap: whether the claim remains excluded after EEOC proceedings terminate.

issue: "No project having a substantial effect on the water resources of the basin" turns approval jurisdiction on an undefined threshold — "substantial effect" — with no measure supplied here or in Article 13. The same is true of the approval test, "substantially impair or conflict with the comprehensive plan."
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “substantial effect” in the jurisdictional sentence and “substantially impair or conflict” in the approval standard, alleging that neither threshold has a supplied measure. Candidate g1 concerns the term “project” and which activities that noun encompasses for purposes of prior approval.
reason: The proposed issue alleges undefined thresholds for substantial effects and substantial impairment or conflict. The candidate instead records ambiguity in the meaning and scope of “project,” so it concerns different words and a different specific defect.

issue: Section 3.8 subjects projects undertaken "by any person, corporation or governmental authority" to review, but Section 1.2(g) defines "project" by reference to work "separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission." Whether private undertakings the commission never identified are within Section 3.8 is only resolvable by reading the two together.
gold_issue: The term “project” in Section 3.8 was lexically ambiguous between Wayne’s and the Commission’s competing interpretations of which activities require prior Commission approval.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns “project” and “by any person, corporation or governmental authority” in Section 3.8, read with Section 1.2(g)’s “separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission.” Candidate g1 concerns the same term, “project” in Section 3.8, and its disputed coverage of activities requiring prior approval.
evidence: I agree with my colleagues that the term "project," as used in Section 3.8 of the Delaware River Basin Compact, is ambiguous, and that the matter should be remanded to the District Court for fact-finding respecting the Compact drafters' intent.
reason: Both identify ambiguity in the scope of “project” and therefore which activities require prior Commission approval. The proposed issue specifies the ambiguity’s source—the interaction with Section 1.2(g) and whether the Commission must have identified a private undertaking—while g1 describes the competing interpretations more broadly.

issue: The eleven-percent rate applies to Albums "sold by PRI for distribution through Normal Retail Channels in the United States," but paragraph 7.06(a) accrues fifty percent of net receipts on licenses of the Master Recordings to third parties. Which provision governs a given exploitation — a sale through a distributor or a license to a third party — is the contest the two provisions set up.
gold_issue: The lower-rate treatment of sales through “Normal Retail Channels” had to be read against § 7.06(a)(ii)’s higher rate for unique and potentially less traceable distribution methods, which confirmed that retail digital downloads belonged in the former category.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue concerns the entire limitation “sold by PRI for distribution through Normal Retail Channels in the United States” and its asserted conflict or boundary with § 7.06(a)’s third-party-license language. Candidate g1 concerns specifically the meaning of “Normal Retail Channels” as applied to iTunes-like downloads, while g2 concerns that phrase and lower-rate sentence read against § 7.06(a)(ii)’s higher-rate distribution categories.
evidence: Applying the 8-15% royalty rate contained in §§ 7.01-7.03 to retail sales of digital downloads, rather than the 50% rate contained in § 7.06(a)(ii), also accords with the structure of the Agreement: For sales to consumers through normal retail channels that are reliably and readily measured, the contract provides for a lower rate; by contrast, as to the unique and, at least potentially, less traceable methods of distribution to consumers listed in § 7.06(a)(ii), the artist, Malmsteen, is assigned a higher rate of compensation.
reason: The proposed issue and g2 both concern the boundary between the lower royalty for normal-retail sales and § 7.06(a)(ii)’s higher royalty for other exploitations, although g2 resolves that boundary specifically for retail digital downloads. The choice was close because g1 addresses the same dispute through the meaning of “Normal Retail Channels,” but g2 more directly records the inter-provision rate contest identified by the proposed issue.

issue: The fifty-percent net-receipts rate is tied to enumerated categories closing with "or by any combination of the methods set forth above or other methods" and "licenses of Master Recordings on a flat-fee basis," so whether a modern third-party distribution licence falls inside the list is a general-versus-specific question. The catch-all sits directly against the enumerated channels.
gold_issue: Malmsteen’s essentially limitless reading of the residual phrase “or other methods” was incoherent with the specifically enumerated distribution methods and the separate record-club subsection because it would render both superfluous.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns principally on “or by any combination of the methods set forth above or other methods” in relation to the enumerated distribution channels, while also mentioning “licenses of Master Recordings on a flat-fee basis.” Candidate g1 turns on the same residual phrase “or other methods” in relation to the specifically enumerated methods and the separate record-club subsection.
evidence: Here, interpreting "or other methods" as Malmsteen does — to be essentially limitless — would render superfluous both the specifically enumerated list in that section and the separate sub-section addressing the sale of Records through record clubs. See Agreement § 7.06(a)(iii).
reason: Both identify the general-versus-specific problem created by reading “or other methods” broadly despite the specifically enumerated distribution methods. The proposed issue broadens the framing by mentioning flat-fee licenses and modern third-party distribution generally, while g1 focuses on digital downloads and the superfluity of the enumerated methods and record-club subsection.

The two royalty regimes cannot both apply and the contract does not say which prevails.
words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “licenses of Master Recordings,” the separate “Net Sale” provisions in §§ 7.02 and 7.05, and the contract’s silence about which royalty regime prevails when both classifications apply. Candidate g1 turns on the residual phrase “or other methods,” its relationship to the specifically enumerated distribution methods, and the separate record-club subsection.

Candidate g1 instead concerns the breadth of “or other methods” within § 7.06(a)(ii) and whether an unlimited reading would nullify the enumerated methods and record-club provision; it is a different defect.

issue: The backstop is triggered by breach of "a representation or warranty set forth in this Section 10 made by Accredited," but Accredited makes no representation in Section 10 — its warranties live in the Accredited Assignment, Assumption and Recognition Agreement, which Exhibit 8 does not reproduce ("Please See Tab #13"). words_at_issue: The proposed issue turns on “a representation or warranty set forth in this Section 10 made by Accredited,” Section 10’s silence as to any such warranties, and the reference to the Accredited Assignment, Assumption and Recognition Agreement in Exhibit 8. The proposed issue adds that the filed Exhibit 8 is not reproduced, but that additional fact does not change the core defect.

The candidate is slightly more specific about the competing “portion” theory and the requirement of a physical part, while the proposed issue additionally mentions the modified construct’s progeny.
